notes.summary: CS143 teaches compilers by building one for Cool, a small object-oriented language. The pipeline — lexing, parsing, semantic analysis, code generation — mirrors what you built in Nand2Tetris projects 10-11 at toy scale. Stanford's course hub (the current edition) runs the same programming assignments that have trained compiler engineers for decades.
concepts: Your N2T compiler as a head start
notes.focus: Write a small Cool program (a class hierarchy with dispatch) this week. The compiler you build must accept what you write — start as its user.

materials.practiceLabel: PA2: the Cool lexer (flex or hand-rolled)

notes.summary: Tokens from text: regexes to NFAs to DFAs (your 18.404J theory, industrialized), longest-match disambiguation, and error handling strategy. The PA2 lexer is your first real pass — and exactly the tokenizer you hand-wrote for N2T project 10, now with a formal guarantee of correctness.
notes.focus: Derive the DFA for a two-rule lexer (identifiers, numbers) by hand through the full pipeline. You have just executed chapters of theory as one exercise.

materials.practiceLabel: PA3: the Cool parser (bison or hand-rolled)

notes.summary: Grammar engineering: derivations, parse trees, ambiguity elimination, left recursion removal, and precedence declarations. The 18.404J CFG theory becomes working code — a parser that rejects invalid programs with precise errors. LL vs LR trade-offs decide hand-written vs generated parsers.
notes.focus: Take an ambiguous expression grammar and fix it with precedence rules, then parse x + y * z by hand. One tree, no ambiguity — that's the assignment's core.

notes.summary: Meaning after structure: attribute grammars decorate the tree, symbol tables track scopes (your CSE341 interpreter knowledge applies directly), and type checking enforces the language's rules. Cool's inheritance graph check (cycles!) is a graph problem — the whole curriculum converges inside the compiler.
notes.focus: Design the symbol table for nested scopes on paper, then trace insert/lookup for a program with shadowing. Your CSE341 environments ARE this structure.

notes.summary: Tree to machine: stack frames for dispatch (your 6.004 activation records, now emitted), object layouts with vtables for dynamic dispatch, and basic code generation strategies for expressions and control flow. The generated MIPS runs in a simulator — closing the loop from source text to machine code you can step through.
notes.focus: Trace one method call in generated MIPS: frame setup, vtable lookup, argument passing, jump, and return. It is your 6.004 stack-frame diagram, now in code YOU emitted.

notes.summary: Making code fast without breaking it: liveness and reaching definitions as fixpoint computations over control-flow graphs, with the worklist algorithm. Dataflow frameworks (meet, transfer, direction) generalize a family of analyses — the mathematical core that LLVM's pass managers implement.
notes.focus: Run liveness to convergence on a 6-block CFG by hand, iterating until NOTHING changes. The stability of the fixpoint is the proof of correctness.

notes.summary: Graph coloring for registers: interference graphs from liveness, k-coloring as allocation, spilling when coloring fails. Then the loop family — induction variables, loop-invariant code motion — the transformations that gave optimizing compilers their name. Spill decisions are where theory meets memory pressure.
notes.focus: Build the interference graph for a small function and 3-color it, spilling one variable. The colors are registers; the spill is a stack slot — now you see them.

notes.summary: The runtime beneath the language: allocation strategies (bump allocation for youth), mark-and-sweep, copying collectors (Cheney's two-space trick), and generational hypotheses. Stop-the-world vs concurrent trade-offs connect to your 6.1810 locking knowledge. Every managed language you use (Python, JS, Go) lives on this lecture.
notes.focus: Trace a copying GC on a heap diagram: copy live objects to to-space, update all pointers. Twelve objects on paper teaches the entire algorithm.

notes.summary: From the classroom to the industry: SSA form (each variable defined once — dataflow for free), LLVM IR as the portable middle layer, and JIT compilation for run-time optimization. This maps your Cool pipeline onto clang, V8, and every modern toolchain — the exact vocabulary of compiler jobs today.
notes.focus: Emit LLVM IR for a small function with clang and read it. You'll recognize YOUR optimizations running as passes — the bridge from class to industry.

lessons.title: Advanced: Type Systems and Certifying Compilers

notes.summary: The theory adjacent to the course: sound type systems as proofs of safety (CSE341's topic, deepened), typed intermediate languages, and certifying compilation where the compiler emits checkable evidence. Rust's borrow checker is this lineage in production — proof techniques shipping in a mainstream compiler.
notes.focus: Write the typing judgment for one Cool expression and explain what bug it makes impossible. Type systems are theorems about your programs — state one.

lessons.title: LR Parsing: LALR and Generated Parsers

notes.summary: Bottom-up parsing: LR(0)/SLR/LALR states built from item sets, shift-reduce decisions driven by tables, and conflict diagnosis when grammars go wrong. Yacc/Bison generate exactly this machinery — and your PA3 experience with generated parsers will now make sense from the inside. The LR family handles more grammars than LL, which is why the industry standard is bottom-up.
notes.focus: Build the LR(0) item sets for a tiny grammar by hand and fill a 2-row parse table. Then parse one string with a stack trace — bottom-up parsing, demystified.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the front half: your lexer, parser, and semantic analyzer running end to end on Cool. The exam style is grammar work and fixpoint tracing — table-driven reasoning you can drill. Re-derive your parser's parse for the trickiest program in your test suite.
notes.focus: Feed one malformed program through your pipeline and fix every error message it produces. Error quality is the difference between a toy and a tool.

notes.summary: The finish: source in, MIPS out, programs running — a compiler YOU built, pass by pass, on top of every course before it (6.100L's expressions, 6.045J's grammars, CSE341's semantics, 6.004's machine model). Your final artifact: the pipeline diagram annotated with which course powers each box. Next, the capstone makes you USE everything.
concepts: What you'd add with more time
notes.focus: Run your compiler on the program you wrote in week 1 and watch it execute. Then draw the annotated pipeline map — it is your entire CS education in one image.
